notes.1a: (i)–(v) Comprehensive responses • Most candidates gave single and precise answers in finding features and identifying them using the key. [Limited responses] • Some candidates incorrectly identified the sports ground as the land-use in part (ii) while others gave the incorrect spot height in part (iv).
notes.1b: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates stated an appropriate six-figure grid reference from quite a wide tolerance given the size of the symbol for the viewpoint. [Limited responses] • Some candidates need to be more accurate when giving a six-figure grid reference, making sure that the third and/or sixth figure are determined correctly. • Some candidates need to make sure they state the eastings and the northings the right way round. �PAGE�12
notes.1c: (i) Comprehensive responses • Candidates correctly identified the compass direction. [Limited responses] • Most candidates need to be more familiar with the 16-point compass and apply it accurately to calculate the compass direction from one point to another, in this case, the two lighthouses. • Most candidates stated the compass direction as north-east which needed to be more precise.
notes.1cii: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates precisely measured the distance using the scale line. • Some candidates correctly stated a distance within the tolerance of 3.1 to 3.4 kilometres. [Limited responses] • Candidates need to be aware of where to place the decimal point in the answer. • Common examples of incorrect responses included 32.5 and 325 kilometres.
notes.1iii: Comprehensive responses • Candidates correctly stated a bearing within the tolerance. [Limited responses] • Some candidates need practice calculating the compass bearing precisely from one point to another, since some responses were just outside the tolerance, while others were a long way from it.
notes.1d: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates suggested two appropriate pieces of evidence, demonstrating accurate interpretation of the map key, using symbols found on the map. [Limited responses] • Some responses were land based, such as sports ground, rather than activities which took place in the sea. • Some responses needed to be linked to tourism, such as harbour and ship.
notes.1e: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates gave two appropriate pieces of map evidence, one each for land and sea travel. • Many candidates recognised that there were no roads crossing the island of Stromboli and therefore looked for alternate means of getting from the south-west to the north-east. [Limited responses] • Some candidates made suggestions that were imprecise, for instance suggesting going on foot. They needed to state the evidence regarding how. • Many suggestions for sea travel were inappropriate, such as by ship, by boat and harbour, because they also needed to specifically refer to map evidence, such as the car ferry.
notes.1f: Comprehensive responses • Looking at the Island as a whole, many candidates correctly described at least two aspects of settlement distribution and were able to relate this to the physical geography. • Common examples included reference to different parts of the island such the north-east and south-west, and referred to coastal, lower and flatter areas. [Limited responses] • Some candidates needed to understand the key term ‘settlement distribution’, because they referred to types of settlement, such as linear or clustered, or were vague, using terms such as uneven. • Some responses misinterpreted the key word settlement as individual types of buildings, leisure and recreational activities, such as guest houses, hotels and churches. �PAGE�13
notes.1g: Comprehensive responses • Some responses correctly described at least three aspects of the relief. These were able to interpret the patterns of the contour lines and spot heights to conclude that the island was both steep and high, and they quoted the height of the highest point. • Some candidates were also able to accurately identify the location of the steeper or gentler slopes. [Limited responses] • A few candidates need to have a more accurate understanding of the key term ‘relief’, because they described human features, such as roads, settlements and tourist attractions. • Some candidates defined gradient with respect to the closeness of the contour lines, rather than describe where gradient differed. • Some candidates need to make sure they always quote units when quoting a height from the map.
notes.2a: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates correctly described two characteristics of the settlement hierarchy usually referring to changes as one moves up or down Table 2.1. For instance, the rural villages have a small population, but this increases further up the hierarchy. • Some candidates linked one numerical variable to another, pointing out the relationship between the two. [Limited responses] • Some candidates needed to make sure their statements referred to the whole hierarchy. For instance, ‘rural areas have the most settlements’, does not describe the number of settlements further up the hierarchy. • Some responses need to make sure the points they make are relevant, thus reference to the number of services at each level is drawn from the candidate’s knowledge and not information derived from Table 2.1. • Some candidates attempted to explain rather than describe the hierarchy. For example, ‘more people live in major urban areas because of better facilities and a higher standard of living’.
notes.2b: (i) Comprehensive responses • Many candidates clearly understood the term ‘function’ as applied to settlements and suggested two relevant functions with appropriate evidence drawn from Figure 2.1. • The evidence was wide-ranging and could be clearly seen on the photograph of Wellington, New Zealand. [Limited responses] • Candidates gave vague answers for example green vegetation, for a relevant function such as tourism. • Candidates should only state evidence that can be seen in Figure 2.1, not what they deduce is present such as hotels (related to the function of tourism). • Some candidates used the same evidence for both functions, such as boats for tourism and port, rather than provide different evidence for each function. • Some suggested vague functions, such as jobs or parking.
notes.2bii: Comprehensive responses • Many candidates suggested two relevant physical factors. • Many physical factors were well linked to its function. [Limited responses] • Many candidates suggested physical factors which were incomplete, such as ‘there is a mountain’ which does not refer to the land being too steep to build on, or that the place is surrounded by mountains for shelter. • Some candidates suggested physical factors which could not be determined from the photograph, such as a fresh water supply. �PAGE�14
notes.3a: Comprehensive responses • Many candidates described three different impacts, using direct observation from Figure 3.1. • There was a mix of impacts both on the physical and human environment. • Some candidates suggested impacts which were not directly seen but could be derived from the photograph such as the water supply being contaminated as a result of the colour of the water. [Limited responses] • Some candidates gave more than one example of the same impact. For example, the roads were cut off, transportation was stopped and there were traffic delays. • Some candidates gave more generic responses, such as infrastructure was damaged, which does not refer specifically to roads.
notes.3b: (i) Comprehensive responses • Many candidates were able to calculate the storm discharge from the storm hydrograph, Figure 3.2, within the given tolerance. [Limited responses] • Some candidates need to ensure greater accuracy, for instance by using a ruler to help read off the value from the Y axis, since they tended to underestimate the storm discharge, such as between 40 and 46 cumecs.
notes.3bii: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates calculated the lag time accurately, a concept with which they seemed familiar. [Limited responses] • Some candidates need to be more accurate when making the calculation. • Some incorrect responses were 8, 11 and 12 hours.
notes.3iii: Comprehensive responses • Some candidates correctly identified two factors which could cause flooding. [Limited responses] • Candidates need to improve their knowledge regarding physical factors which are responsible for flooding, since many identified gentle slopes and/or a large drainage basin as the cause.
notes.3iv: Comprehensive responses • Some responses correctly identified a way. [Limited responses] • Many candidates were not familiar with the hydrological cycle and answered for example, steep slopes, tributaries, glaciers and dams. • Many responses gave factors which contribute to surface runoff, rather than answered the question.
notes.4a: (i) Comprehensive responses • Many responses stated a correct definition. [Limited responses] • Some responses were vague, such as ‘areas where the earthquake reaches’, and ‘where the earthquake is strongest’.
notes.4aii: Comprehensive responses • Some responses stated a correct definition. �PAGE�15 0460 Geography March 2026 [Limited responses] • Many responses gave the definition of the focus having got the two definitions for an earthquake’s focus and epicentre the wrong way round. • Many responses gave a partial definition, such as ‘directly above the focus’, which also needed to refer to the earth’s surface. • Some responses were imprecise, for example, ‘above the earth’s surface’; some responses were inaccurate, for example, ‘where the earthquake is greatest’.
notes.4b: Comprehensive responses • Many candidates provided a range of different explanations which addressed all three resources. • Some candidates discussed a course of events in which further implications were stated. For instance, for Figure 4.3 it was suggested that people would not be able to go to work due to the road being blocked ‘which would lead people making long diversions’ and/or ‘this would cause traffic congestion’. [Limited responses] • Some candidates gave more than one example of the same effect on local people, such as references to people being killed or injured, or giving more than one reference to job losses, these responses needed to show and explain a wider range of effects. • Some candidates gave a description (which was not a command word in the question) before the explanation, such as ‘the school has collapsed’ or ‘the road has a large crack along it due to the earthquake’. • For Figure 4.1, many candidates needed to read the title of the photograph more carefully, because they referred to the effects on housing and not the school. • For Figure 4.2, some candidates needed to pay more attention to the key terms in the question, because they referred to the impact on tourists not on local people.
notes.5a: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates described several relevant features of the farm in Figure 5.1. • They employed a range of appropriate geographical terminology in their descriptions. [Limited responses] • Some candidates described a few relevant features. • Some responses described features which were not present, for example machinery, or which could not be determined from Figure 5.1 such as ‘drip irrigation is taking place’ or ‘the soil is fertile’. Candidates should focus only on features they can observe. • Some responses were vague, such as there is a wall, or a lot of greenery is found. Candidates should state how these are part of the farming system, for instance ‘the wall surrounds the farm and provides shelter’.
notes.5b: (i) Comprehensive responses • Some candidates clearly stated two relevant differences either by using comparative terms or describing each farm in turn using certain criteria, for example size or the number of different crops grown. [Limited responses] • Many responses partly addressed the question. • Many candidates stated how the land is used in Figure 5.2, but not in Figure 5.1, such as ‘the farm in Figure 5.2 is large’, or ‘the farm only grows one crop’. Where a question asks for differences then candidates should identify this as a key term and be prepared to use comparative statements. �PAGE�16
notes.5bii: Comprehensive responses • Some candidates gave two relevant reasons which demonstrated an understanding of how the production of a single crop which is usually for export, can mean there is a shortage of land and food for local people. [Limited responses] • Many responses were incomplete and needed further explanation, Statements such as ‘only one crop is grown’, should be more specific about the case of sugar cane, and ‘the land is over cultivated’, needs to refer to the impact on soil quality. • Some responses introduced factors which were not relevant, such as ‘a change in the weather damages the crop so there will no food to eat’, and ‘disease could destroy the whole crop’.
notes.6a: Comprehensive responses • Many candidates correctly completed the pie chart, Figure 6.1, accurately using appropriate shading in the correct order from the key. [Limited responses] • Some candidates incorrectly drew a line outside the tolerance. • Some candidates completed the figure in the wrong order, because the services were placed to the right of the agriculture sector. • A few candidates did not use correct shading, such as the dashes for industry not being horizontal or the diagonal lines for services being incorrect by 90°.
notes.6b: (i) Comprehensive responses • Many candidates gave a correct definition of secondary industry. [Limited responses] • Some responses referred to the service sector rather than the secondary sector. • Some responses referred to the use of labour, without referring to secondary industry.
notes.6bii: Comprehensive responses • Some candidates stated a method which was appropriate for a map. [Limited responses] • Many candidates did not state a method applied to a map, such as ‘bar graphs’ suggesting they need to read the question more carefully. • Some candidates gave vague answers, such as ‘colouring’, or ‘shading’ rather than suggest a named technique.
notes.6iii: Comprehensive responses • Some responses comprehensively evaluated the location using the features shown in Figure 6.2 in a National Park setting as a stimulus. This resulted in a range of both economic advantages and environmental disadvantages. [Limited responses] • Many candidates described some appropriate advantages and/or disadvantages. • Some points needed to be more clearly linked to Figure 6.1. for instance, it was stated by some candidates that woodchips were easy to export, the responses then needed to explain whether this would be done by sea or ship. • Some candidates suggested that economic advantages would occur because of increased tourism due to the wood chip industry, which was inappropriate. • Candidates needed to state the source of pollution, such as dust from processing of wood chips, or the impact on the environment, such as the wildlife being disturbed by noise. �PAGE�17
notes.key_messages:
What candidates did well
• Most candidates were able to locate features on a map accurately and identify them using the key.
• The concept of relief was understood by most candidates resulting in contour patterns and other relief
features being recognised.
• Most candidates were able to make valid statements about the distribution of settlements from the
topographical map.
• Most candidates were able to interpret photographic resources correctly with respect to the
requirements of the question (Questions 2(b), 3(a), 4(b), 5 and 6(b)(iii)).
• Comprehensive responses fully addressed the question’s requirements, using skills such as description
from observation, explanation and evaluation.
What candidates needed to improve
• Some candidates need to be more precise when measuring distance, directions and bearings on a
• Some candidates need to take greater care when measuring angles on a pie chart and making simple
calculations from graphs.
• Some candidates need to demonstrate a greater understanding of key terms when giving a definition
for example in Questions 4(a)(i) and (ii).
• Some candidates need to read questions carefully and ensure their answers directly address what is
being asked; for example, Question 4(b) referred to ‘local people’ and not tourists.
• Many responses repeated the same ideas for instance reference to injury for each of Figures 4.1, 4.2
and 4.3 in Question 4(b).
• When interpreting photographs candidates should refer to what they can observe, not what is not
